claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has an inherently heterogeneous ferrite-pearlite microstructure.
Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a native thin surface oxide layer.
High-temperature salt exposure promotes rapid, non-uniform growth of iron oxide scales on untreated Q235 steel.
The high-temperature iron oxide scales are porous.
The high-temperature iron oxide scales are poorly adherent and prone to spallation.
Porous, spalling iron oxide provides little long-term corrosion protection.
Oxidation of salt-exposed Q235 steel proceeds more slowly at room temperature than at 700–900 °C.
Room-temperature exposure produces a thinner and relatively stable oxide film.
The relatively cohesive room-temperature oxide film slows further degradation.
At elevated temperature, faster oxidation combined with salt-induced fluxing disrupts formation of a continuous, self-healing oxide scale.
Spallation repeatedly exposes fresh Q235 steel to corrosive attack.
Salt-exposed Q235 steel at 700–900 °C will show greater mass loss than salt-exposed Q235 steel at room temperature.
High-temperature samples will show deeper oxide penetration than room-temperature samples.
Microscopy will reveal more discontinuous and spalled oxide layers after high-temperature exposure.
The room-temperature oxide layer will be more uniform than the high-temperature oxide layer.
The proposed mechanism should apply when Q235 steel lacks alloying additions capable of forming more protective passivating oxides.
Pretreatment or alloying that produces a stable, adherent oxide can prevent the proposed degradation mechanism from applying.
Mass loss, spallation, and oxide microstructure will depend on surface finish and salt composition.
